crux.for_the_english: Keep the syntax drifting where hers drifts: the long, additive sentences, the repeated returns to the same few words — far, quiet, smile, tiredness, dream, nostalgia (懐かしみ), forgiveness (許し), peace/rest (安らかさ) — and do not vary them for elegance. Keep the vision grammatically and referentially unfixed: we are not told who the three are, where they are, or whether this is old age, death, or a picture in her eyes. In particular, do not turn あの日 / その日 into 'heaven', 'when we die', or 'someday when things get better'. The husband must not be made to understand what he has not understood; the closing resolve to work, clear up, and get up early must stay deliberately smaller and more practical than her vision.
crux.point: The crux is time seen from its far end. A mouthful of badly cooked potato — cold, hard, gritty, tasteless in the middle of an otherwise warm supper — suddenly detaches the young mother from the present, and she sees her marriage's poverty, fear, illness, and exhaustion as if from a vast distance after it has all passed, when suffering will have become 'nostalgia and forgiveness'. The shock the text keeps returning to is measurable and must not be softened: only three years have passed (p14, p22–27), yet inside the life it feels interminable and she feels already old (p13). Her vision (p16–17) is not a plan or an escape fantasy so much as a change of tense: the present, looked at as already past and forgiven, becomes bearable, and she can come back to the table, smile, and agree to keep working (p20, p34–35). A translation that explains this — as a daydream, a premonition of death, religious consolation, or marital hopefulness — will make it smaller and clearer than it is.
crux.why: Everything structural serves that slippage. The story barely moves: a storm outside, a crowded table cleared so the baby cannot grab things, a meal begun, a potato tasted, a husband twice asking why she is silent, a brief exchange counting the years, the child fed and put to the breast, the table to be cleared. Against that stillness the interior passages lengthen and loosen, subjects drop away, and 'she remembered / she was seeing' shades into a picture that is at once in her eyes, in the future, and in a dim light with three quiet figures telling an endless story that contains all good and evil, grief, anger, and joy while no one moves and everyone smiles (p16). The comfort is inseparable from its strangeness: what consoles her is not that suffering will stop soon — the dialogue at the end admits it will not — but that from far enough away it will no longer need to be answered.

open_questions.question: Are the three figures in the vision the family grown old, the family after death, or an deliberately unidentifiable trio? The text gives three people, bowed heads, nostalgia and forgiveness as if before an eternal, night-like rest — suggestive of age and death but never naming either. The editor needs to rule how much, if at all, the English may lean toward the funereal; my reading is to lean not at all.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the figures become 'themselves as an old couple' or 'in the afterlife', the vision hardens into doctrine and the final return to work loses its odd, unresolved consolation.

open_questions.question: The baby is explicitly a girl (女の子, p2; 彼女, p7), yet both parents address her as 坊や, literally 'little boy' but usable as a fond generic for a baby. Render as 'baby', a name-like 'little one', or keep 'boy' with the contradiction visible?
open_questions.why_it_matters: 'Boy' in English will read as an authorial error or a bible inconsistency; 'baby' loses the period, colloquial warmth of the address and the way it punctuates the parents' delight at p8, p29–30.

open_questions.question: How eschatological is あの日 / 安息? 安息 can be ordinary rest or eternal rest. Is her 'day when everything changes into nostalgia and forgiveness' a day in this life (old age looking back), the approach of death, or intentionally both?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This governs single words at the story's summit — 'rest', 'repose', 'peace', 'that day' — and whether the ending reads as endurance within life or as quietly longing for its end.

data.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the translation must be able to come back to it: the story opens on the storm as a bare perception ('Outside the now-dark door, a violent sound of rain and wind — a storm', p1) and ends with the husband stopped still, whispering the same fact ('It's a storm', p38). In between, the family is for a while too noisy and absorbed to hear it at all (p8), and the wife hears it again, quietly, at exactly the moment she re-enters her vision after her husband's first question (p19). The storm is not a symbol to be underlined; it is the outside world and the passing of the evening, first unnoticed, then registered from inside her distance. Keep its three appearances plain and verbally linked, and keep the final line bare and unadorned — nothing has been solved, the child is simply asleep at the breast and the room has gone quiet.

The opening supper needs its full physical warmth and disorder, because the vision only detaches from something solid. The parents are young and unwrinkled but already worn (p3): tiredness in his hollowed, gentle eyes, a deeper tiredness and a sleepy peace about her hair and shoulders. Their tenderness is enacted, not stated — everything grabbable moved under the table, the baby drumming spoon and plate, the father's whole face breaking into a smile he tries to contain while he feeds her and crams rice into his own mouth in the gaps, the parents laughing at each other over the child (p5–10). Do not ennoble this into glowing poverty or cuteness, and do not flatten it either: the baby's chubby roundness, long lashes, quick clever hands, the big red hand, the steam off the rice, the deep blue pot of beef and onion, carrot and potato, are the counterweight. If this half is thinned, her stillness at the potato will look like the story's default mood rather than a fall out of shared life.

The potato itself (p10–12) must stay oddly literal. It is not merely disappointing: bitten expecting it sweet and soft, it is as if frozen, hard and gritty (ざくざく), profoundly tasteless, and she re-bites it with her front teeth in surprise. The text insists on the tastelessness as 無味, unrelated (かかはりのない) and cold, and it is that unrelated quality that gives her 'a quiet, lonely, far-away heart'. Resist making the potato 'symbolise' her marriage in the English; the Japanese lets a contingent, almost accidental sensation open the distance, and the slight disproportion is the point. Likewise keep the sequence of her remembering unsorted — days of tears, days threatened and frightened over material things, days of illness, all already dreamlike and even the suffering nostalgic while she remembers it (p13) — rather than rationalising it into a summary of three hard years.

Her register is the story's main technical risk. Shizu's prose in the interior sections is repetitive, incantatory and syntactically loose, circling: ながい物語り 'a long story told without ceasing', then ながい生活、ながい悲しみ、ながい苦しみ in p20; 静か, 遠い, なつかしみ, 許し, 安らかさ recurring as a small chord rather than a developing argument. Berman's usual deformations are all waiting here: clarification (naming the three figures, explaining the day), expansion (adding connective reasoning between the potato, the memory, the vision and the smile), ennoblement (lifting her plain vision into lyrical transcendence), and destroying the network of repetitions by elegantly varying 'long', 'quiet', 'far' and 'smile'. The couple's dialogue offers some protection and must keep its own plainness and slight non-sequitur: 'Why are you so quiet?' — 'It really has been only a little while, hasn't it, since we married' (p21–22). She is not answering his question; she is bringing the vision's arithmetic back into the room. His answering count — just three years, and yet we've suffered; in a while the baby will walk (p25, p28) — is fond, practical, and knowingly inadequate. Do not harmonise the two registers into one shared understanding. The story ends not in communion about the vision, which he never hears, but in parallel resolve: his 'It won't be much longer' (もう少しの間だ, p34) spoken almost to himself, her calm 'Then let us work' (p35), clearing up and early rising tomorrow (p36). Her hope, if that is the word, is private, disproportionate, and returns as housework and sleep.

A few smaller things the translator should watch. The child is a baby girl who can just stand holding the table, yet the parents call her 坊や; see the open questions rather than silently fixing it. The marriage's three years are stated three times in different keys (narrated at p14, marvelled at by her at p22 and p27, confirmed by him at p25); keep all three, since the repetition is the measure of the distortion. The vision's story-within is told by and to the three figures across what seems a lifetime; avoid past-tense summary that makes it safely concluded — it is still going on, no one moves, the smile continues (p16). Finally, watch the smiles: the word 微笑/笑み belongs to the laughing parents at the table, to the unmoving figures in the vision, and to the wife alone as she comes back from it (p20) and turns to her husband 'as if with nostalgia' (p21). Varying or dropping it where it recurs will break the thin thread by which the supper and the vision are, quietly, the same scene seen at two distances.
data.say: I can read the broad movement with confidence, but I cannot settle from the text alone whether the vision in p16–18 is meant as old age, death, or a deliberately timeless elsewhere; nor whether 坊や for a baby explicitly called a girl is ordinary period usage or a marked choice. I have flagged both rather than resolving them in the reading.

voice_takes.label: spare_and_close
voice_takes.line: Spare and close: short, plain English, repetitions kept even at the cost of awkwardness; the vision left unexplained.

voice_takes.label: warm_domestic
voice_takes.line: Warmer and more idiomatic at the table — fuller dialogue, softer interior prose — risking some smoothing of her drift into lyricism.

voice_takes.label: formal_taisho
voice_takes.line: Slightly formal, period-held narrative diction, slower cadence throughout, matching the 1917 surface without archaising the dialogue.
